newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Iraqi crude not expected in Asia until January.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi crude not expected in Asia until January.

text.p: Iraqi crude oil is not likely to hit Asia until January due to problems at Iraq's Mina al-Bakr terminal and the reluctance of regional refiners to lift the crude at such short notice, industry sources said on Tuesday.

"The lines and equipment at the terminal are not totally acceptable. Some of the pipelines have rusted and corroded and need to be replaced," a source close to the United Nations (UN) appointed inspectorate from the Dutch-based Saybolt company said.

The source, speaking as Iraqi President Saddam Hussein was reported to have pushed a button to resume exports after a six-year break since the Gulf War, said repair works would probably be done very fast.

The Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr is Iraq's main export point for crude oil shipments to Asia but the bulk of its exports are to be channelled through Turkey's Ceyhan which is linked by pipeline to th Iraqi oil centre in Kirkuk.
Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said earlier that Iraq would begin pumping 650,000 barrels of crude oil on Tuesday from Kirkuk to Turkey.

Rasheed also said oil would start flowing through the Mina al-Bakr terminal on Friday or Saturday. Iraq intended to ship about 350,000 barrels per day of crude from the terminal, oil ministry senior undersecretary Taha Hmud Mosa said.
But trading sources in Singapore said they had been told that exports from the terminal would not be ready until the end of December and have not been notified of any change to the schedule.
"According to the schedule of work, oil should not pump out until end December," a source at a Japanese trading house said.
The UN on Monday said it had dispatched 14 independent inspection agents from Saybolt to the the Mina al-Bakr oil terminal, the pipeline metering station near Zakho and the Ceyhan oil terminal.
Traders also said that even if crude oil was available for loading in December it is very unlikely that any refiner can lift it at such short notice.
"Refiners are not rushing in to buy as most have covered their requirements for even up to January." one crude oil trader who is in touch with Iraq said.
"We are requesting for crude oil in February but they (Iraq) are asking us to take in January," said one source at a trading company which is negotiating with Iraq.
Under the oil-for-food program concluded in May but held up by disputes with the U.N., Iraq will be able to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy humanitarian goods.

Among the Asian companies in discussions with Iraq to lift crude oil are Caltex Petroleum Corp, the joint venture between U.S. major Texaco Inc and Chevron Corp, Cosmo Oil Co Ltd, Mitsubishi Corp and Itochu Corp .
Iraq will export Basrah Light crude from Mina al-Bakr which has been priced to Asian buyers at a 20 cents premium to the average of benchmark Middle East crudes -- Oman and Dubai.
Traders said the price was attractive as it is lower than the comparable Saudi Arabian Light crude at a 75 cents premium to the Oman and Dubai average quotations.
